title: Halim
subtitle: Persian wheat and lamb porridge
excerpt: Halim is a Persian slow-cooked porridge of pearl barley (or wheat berries), lamb, and warm spices, cooked low and slow until the grain and meat break down into a thick, creamy, almost homogenous porridge. It is a winter breakfast and a ritual food, eaten with butter, cinnamon, and date syrup.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Halim documented as a ritual breakfast food prepared overnight for special occasions. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). The slow cooking method and the service with sweet toppings described.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring to prevent sticking.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large pot. It keeps in the fridge for three days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Halim is typically cooked overnight on the lowest setting. Start it the evening before for a breakfast or brunch the next day.

content.text: Halim is a Persian slow-cooked porridge of pearl barley and lamb cooked together for several hours until they collapse into a smooth, thick, savoury porridge. It is eaten warm for breakfast, topped with melted butter, ground cinnamon, and date syrup, which transforms the savoury base into something sweet-salty and deeply comforting. The long cooking does all the work; it requires only occasional stirring.

items.prepNote: bone-in if possible, cut into large pieces

content.text: Put {{pearl-barley}}, {{lamb-shoulder}}, {{onion}}, {{turmeric-ground}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{black-pepper}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, and 1.5 litres of water in a large heavy pot. Bring to the boil, skimming any foam that rises.

Reduce to the lowest possible heat, cover tightly, and cook for two and a half to three hours. Stir every thirty minutes and add more water if the porridge looks dry. It should remain looser than you want it as it thickens on standing.
After two and a half hours, remove the lamb pieces. Pull the meat from the bones and shred it finely. Discard the bones, onion, and any large pieces of fat.

Return the shredded lamb to the pot. Using a wooden spoon or the back of a ladle, beat the mixture vigorously for two to three minutes to break down the barley into a smooth, thick porridge. Taste and adjust salt.
Ladle into bowls. Top each serving with a knob of {{unsalted-butter}}, a generous drizzle of {{date-syrup}}, and a pinch of ground cinnamon. Eat while hot.

items.symptom: The barley hasn't broken down after three hours
items.cause: Heat was too low or not enough liquid
items.fix: Turn up the heat slightly and cook for another 30 minutes. The barley should eventually dissolve. Beat more vigorously with the spoon at the end.

items.symptom: The halim is sticking and burning at the base
items.cause: Too little liquid or heat too high
items.fix: Add 200 ml of boiling water and stir the base well to lift any sticking. Reduce the heat further and stir more frequently.

items.cause: The sweet toppings are essential, not optional
items.fix: The combination of the savoury porridge with date syrup and cinnamon is what makes halim. Do not skip the toppings.

items.symptom: The texture is grainy rather than smooth
items.cause: Not beaten vigorously enough at the end
items.fix: Beat with a wooden spoon for at least three minutes. The starch in the barley needs to be broken down and worked smooth.

content.text: Halim is eaten across a wide stretch from Iran and Afghanistan through Pakistan into South Asia, where it is called haleem. All versions share the same idea: grain and meat slow-cooked into a thick porridge. The Persian version is a breakfast food, linked to Ramadan, when large pots are cooked overnight to be eaten at sahoor (the pre-dawn meal) or shared with neighbours. The sweet toppings of butter, cinnamon, and date syrup set the Persian version apart. The South Asian version is savoury, finished with ghee and crispy onions.
